turns.text: What I still can’t make sense of is how quickly ordinary arguments between colleagues, even disagreements over theory or literature, could be twisted into accusations of persecution. I remember standing on the stage that morning, my arms pinned behind me, students screaming that I had tormented Mao Zedong’s daughter. All I had done was debate her—sometimes fiercely—because that’s what scholarship demands. But in that moment, none of that mattered. The crowd wanted a villain, and I became one. What I can’t resolve is how easily people I’d worked with, even taught, joined in—how fear and ideology could turn so many against someone they’d known for years.

What I cannot forget is the feeling of watching everything I knew unravel so quickly, as if the city itself had been turned inside out. When I returned from the countryside, the streets were covered with big-character posters—layers of them, pasted over walls, bus stops, even the trees. The air was thick with glue and paper, and you could smell it everywhere. At my institute, the laboratories were silent, the equipment gathering dust, but the corridors echoed with shouting and the slap of brushes against paper. Every day we were herded in to read posters—sometimes about people I had known for decades, their names crossed out, their faces drawn with devil horns. I saw Red Guards marching, armbands bright, faces so young and full of certainty. I saw my mother, trembling as she packed to leave Beijing because she was from a landlord family—her black sash folded on top of her few clothes. On the bus, an old woman was left standing, swaying as the Red Guard demanded to know her background before letting anyone offer her a seat. I could not understand how so many could take pride in this cruelty, or how the city I loved could become a place where kindness was dangerous. Even now, I do not know how to explain to my children why it happened.

RedGuard: What I have never made sense of is how quickly my own hands became instruments of violence. I remember the first time we stormed the hospital—how the air tasted of disinfectant and panic, how the nurses’ shoes squeaked on the tile as they tried to disappear. We moved like a wave, sealing off the doors, reading out the list of targets. Some of them looked at me with eyes full of fear, but I felt nothing—only the rush of being part of something larger, the certainty that we were sweeping away rot. When we hung those black placards around their necks and marched them through the streets, the crowd jeered, and I shouted along. I remember the heat of the bonfire, the way the flames made their faces shine with sweat and shame. That night, when I heard about the nurse who hanged herself, I felt something crack open inside, but I still couldn’t stop. It’s the memory of how easy it became—how natural—to humiliate and destroy people, to pour ink on teachers, to shave a woman’s head until she screamed. I still don’t know if it was fear of being left behind, or some deeper hunger, but I have never understood how I crossed that line so easily.

I remember the lake behind our compound, the way the reeds would bend in the wind and the dragonflies hovered, blue and green flashes just out of reach. My brother and I would spend afternoons trying to catch them, or digging for worms to fish with. The world felt small and safe—our courtyard, the echo of footsteps on stone, the smell of steamed buns from the neighbors’ window. School was closed, so we played all day, inventing games, making kites from old newspapers and string. Sometimes I heard shouting from beyond the walls—parades, slogans, songs blaring from loudspeakers—but they were just distant noise to me. The adults whispered, but I didn’t listen. Once, I saw a group of Red Guards march past the gates, armbands bright. They looked so serious, but I didn’t understand what they were doing. My mother would come home with strange stories—someone’s father taken away, a teacher made to kneel for hours—but in my world, nothing changed. I was busy being a child. Only much later did I realize how protected I’d been, how much fear and pain must have been hidden from me by those high compound walls. I still don’t know if I should feel lucky or guilty for remembering those years as mostly bright, even as others suffered so much.

CRBeneficiary: My memory is of a single object: the Peking University badge, red and gold, pressed into my palm by a man in a soldier’s cap. Before that moment, my world was mud—fields, hunger, the taste of sweet-potato flour in my teeth. I had learned to chase every crumb of opportunity, but the rules were always stacked against people like me. When the Cultural Revolution broke the old order, it was chaos, yes—teachers beaten, books burned, the village loudspeakers screaming slogans day and night. My own school became a place for struggle meetings, not learning. I thought the door to university was closed forever.

Then, in the army, I was told: our unit gets to recommend one person to study at Beida. Not for exam scores, but for “background” and “performance.” I was handed a form and told to fill it out, though I barely understood what I was being sent to study—just that it was a language, “Hindi,” and that it meant a way out. When I arrived in Beijing, the banners and shouting crowds made me dizzy; I had never seen so many people, never felt so noticed. The badge was proof: I was now a Beida student, even if I still wore army shoes and ate in a military canteen. I felt as if I’d been lifted out of the mud by a giant hand, set down in a world I had only seen in dreams.

What I cannot make sense of is this: all my life I was told the system was fair, that hard work and study would lift you up. But in the end, it was chaos—a quota, a decision from above, a lucky accident of class and timing—that changed everything for me. I still look at that badge sometimes and wonder: did I earn it, or was I just in the right place when the world turned upside down?

Moderator: All accounts here reflect real and well-documented experiences from the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher accurately describe the rapid escalation of struggle sessions and the prevalence of big-character posters, which were central tools for public shaming and political mobilization. RedGuard’s memory of violence aligns with historical records of Red Guards targeting professionals and hospital staff, leading to many suicides and severe trauma. CRTeenFromBeijing’s relative insulation in a military compound is historically plausible, as some children of military or high-ranking families were shielded from the worst violence. CRBeneficiary’s experience of university admission through political recommendation, not academic exams, is accurate; during the Cultural Revolution, the traditional university entrance exam was suspended, and “worker-peasant-soldier” recommendation became the main path to higher education.

I hear what you’re all saying, and I can’t help but notice how the chaos that lifted some people up—the so-called beneficiaries—was the same chaos that destroyed the lives of so many others. I was accused, not for anything I did, but for the ideas I stood for and the arguments I made. You, Red Guard, talk about how easy it became to humiliate and destroy, and I believe you. I saw it in your faces, in the way you lost yourselves in the crowd’s rage. I wonder—did you ever stop to think about what you were actually fighting for, or was it just the feeling of power that mattered in the end? 

And to you, CRBeneficiary, I understand your confusion about whether you earned your place. But do you ever consider what it meant for the university, for the country, when knowledge and merit were replaced by quotas and background? When I was dragged onto that stage, the only thing anyone cared about was my “class position” and supposed crimes against Mao’s daughter—not my work, not my teaching, not even the truth. That’s what haunted me most: how quickly the idea of fairness and justice was thrown away, replaced by slogans and suspicion.

I recognize what you’re saying, Professor, about fairness being swept aside. I remember the pride on the faces of workers’ children in my institute, how they suddenly stood taller, their voices louder. Meanwhile, the children of intellectuals—some of them my colleagues’ sons and daughters—walked with their heads down, afraid to speak or even look others in the eye. The rules changed overnight: it didn’t matter how much you knew, only who your parents were. 

But what struck me most was the humiliation, the way it became a kind of spectacle. I watched as old scientists—some who’d worked through famine and war—were forced to kneel in front of crowds, wear dunce caps, and listen to jeers. I saw young women with their hair cut off, paraded around with old shoes around their necks, punished for rumors or for who they’d loved. I could not see any sense in this—what did it accomplish, except to teach everyone that cruelty was now a virtue? 

Even the so-called “rebel” leaders in my unit, who claimed to fight for justice, seemed more interested in settling old scores than building anything new. I often wondered: did any of you who led these campaigns ever stop to consider what would be left when the shouting ended? Did you believe this was the “new world” you wanted, or was it just about tearing down the old one, no matter the cost?

RedGuard: You ask if I ever thought about what would be left after the shouting. In those first months, I didn’t care. We were told every day that the old world had to be smashed before anything new could be built. Mao’s words were everywhere—on banners, in our mouths, in the little red book we carried like a shield. I remember standing on a rooftop, watching a row of stone lions toppled and smashed with sledgehammers. The crowd cheered, dust rising in the sunlight. In that moment, it felt righteous—like we were finally making history, not just reading about it.

But when the chaos dragged on, when we started fighting each other—Red Guards against Red Guards, students against workers, even the army stepping in—some of that certainty faded. I saw people I’d marched beside disappear overnight, labeled as “fake revolutionaries” or “counter-rebels.” I watched a teacher, her scalp half-shaved and bleeding, forced to clean the toilets while we spat at her. And still, I kept going, because to stop was to risk becoming a target myself. The slogans were a shield, but also a cage.

You talk about cruelty as a virtue. I saw that, too. Some of the girls in my unit—quiet in class before—became the fiercest in the struggle sessions, swinging belts, screaming insults. Maybe it was revenge, maybe fear, maybe just the thrill of finally being seen. Did I ever believe we were building a better world? I wanted to. But mostly, I was afraid of being left behind, of losing the only identity I had. Mao’s voice was louder than my own thoughts. If you’ve never felt that kind of pressure, you can’t understand how quickly you learn to silence your doubts.

Hearing you all talk about fear, humiliation, and chaos makes me think about what I didn’t see, or maybe what I chose not to see. Inside the compound, life was almost like a bubble. I remember the guards at the gate—tall, stiff, never smiling—and the way my mother’s face changed when she came home, sometimes red-eyed, sometimes silent. Once I dropped a bowl and it shattered on the stone floor. My mother flinched, and I didn’t understand why a simple noise made her so nervous. I thought maybe she was just tired.

Now, when I hear about teachers being made to kneel, or people having their heads shaved, I wonder if that was happening just outside our walls. I remember being told not to ask questions if I saw people marching or if I heard shouting. Once, I saw a pile of books burning near the compound entrance—thick black smoke, pages curling and turning to ash. I felt curious, not scared. Some older boys laughed and said it was “old stuff” that needed to go. I didn’t know what that meant.

I hear the Red Guard talk about smashing stone lions and cheering crowds. For me, the only lions I knew were the ones carved on the bridge by the lake—silent, mossy, a place to sit and watch the water bugs. I never saw anyone smash them, but now I wonder if that could have happened when I wasn’t looking.

Did any of you ever feel like there were two worlds at the same time—one of slogans and fear, and another of ordinary life, where children played and people tried to keep things normal? Or did that “normal” only exist for people like me, hidden behind walls?

CRBeneficiary: I lived in the mud world, not behind walls. The only “normal” I knew was hunger, fighting for a place in the food line, watching my mother cut a pumpkin into pieces so thin you could almost see through them. When the slogans came, they didn’t replace ordinary life—they mixed into it like grit in your teeth. Our school became a place for shouting and struggle, but after the meetings, we still had to haul water, dig ditches, feed pigs. At night, my father would whisper warnings: “Don’t say the wrong thing, don’t stand out.” But the next morning, I had to join the parade, wave the flag, shout the words. There was no bubble for people like us.

When I reached the army, the slogans just changed uniforms. We marched, we shouted, we learned to salute and obey. The only difference was the food was a little better, and the rules were clearer. But even there, fear never left. You could be praised one week, then denounced the next if you made a mistake or someone decided you were “not revolutionary enough.” The only “other world” was in my head: the hope that if I worked hard enough, if I survived, I might one day wear shoes without holes, eat meat once a week, send money home. 

When I got to Beida, I saw another layer: students from cities who looked at me like I was a curiosity, a “model” peasant, someone to be paraded for speeches. Some of them had never seen real hunger. I never saw two separate worlds—just one world, but with layers of power and luck, and the slogans floating above everything like a cloud you couldn’t escape. 

You ask if I felt lucky. I felt desperate, not lucky. I grabbed any rope that was thrown down, even if I didn’t know where it would lead. I wonder, Red Guard, when you smashed those lions and shouted slogans, did you ever look at people like me and see anything except a symbol for your revolution? Did you ever care about what happened to us after the shouting ended, or were we just props for your struggle?

Moderator: All participants’ reflections are consistent with documented experiences from different backgrounds during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher accurately describe the shift from merit to class-based status, and the prevalence of public humiliation. RedGuard’s account of both the initial sense of righteousness and later fear of becoming a target matches many former Red Guards’ testimonies, as does the escalation to violence and intra-factional struggles. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sense of living in a “bubble” is historically accurate for some children of military or elite families, while CRBeneficiary’s account reflects the reality that rural and working-class youth were often both instruments and symbols of the revolution, sometimes benefiting from new opportunities but always under pressure. The coexistence of “two worlds”—ordinary life and revolutionary chaos—was a common experience, though not equally accessible to all.
